source.title: Rethinking Evaluation of Sparse Autoencoders through the Representation of Polysemous Words
source.authors: Gouki Minegishi; Hiroki Furuta; Yusuke Iwasawa; Yutaka Matsuo

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses polysemantic neurons as motivation, but its experiments evaluate sparse-autoencoder (SAE) feature representations of polysemous words. It does not measure whether individual neurons respond to unrelated inputs or test any of the listed versions.
record.gate_note: The measured outcomes concern SAE features and the paper's PS-Eval metric, not individual neurons in trained networks. Those results are recorded as related findings under fits_no_version. Background claims and results cited from other work are not rows.
record.test_reason: The paper evaluates SAE features on polysemous words (PS-Eval). It invokes polysemantic neurons and superposition only as motivation. It never measures whether individual neurons in a vision or language model respond to unrelated inputs, what share of neurons do so, or what causes it. Its results concern SAE dictionary quality, a related but different construct.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that PS-Eval measures whether SAE features separate word senses. Larger dictionaries help up to a limit. MSE-L0-optimized activation functions (TopK, JumpReLU) do not improve semantic extraction (ReLU > JumpReLU > TopK). Deeper layers and attention outputs show higher specificity. The paraphrase omits the activation-function finding.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes and applies PS-Eval to SAE feature activations for polysemous word contexts; it does not reproduce the original neuron-example analysis or the SoLU study's method.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported SAE evaluation varies expansion ratio, SAE layer, activation function, training data domain, transformer component, and base model. The authors note that maximum-activation scoring may not always align with word meaning.

fits_no_version.finding: On GPT-2 small, SAE features separate different-meaning contexts of a polysemous token more than raw activations do (cosine distance, figure only).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features distinguish polysemous word senses better than base-model activation vectors.

fits_no_version.finding: PS-Eval accuracy rises with expansion ratio, saturating around 64 (layer 4: 0.6005 to 0.6669). For the SAE itself, ReLU beats JumpReLU and TopK on F1.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE semantic-disentanglement scores depend on dictionary size and activation function, not tracking MSE-L0.

fits_no_version.finding: SAE specificity is higher in deeper layers and on attention outputs. Open SAEs for Pythia-70M and Gemma2-2B score lower than for GPT-2 small.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sense separation by SAE features varies with layer, component and base model.

record.problems: The paper itself notes that using only the maximum-activated SAE feature can produce edge cases and that the top feature may reflect aspects unrelated to the target word's meaning. Many reported comparisons are shown only in figures without numeric values. The WiC-based evaluation covers word-meaning distinctions and does not directly measure individual-neuron polysemanticity.
record.rows_left_out: Other SAE-metric outcomes, including activation-function comparisons (Tables 11–13), training-domain comparisons (Figure 8), random and dense SAE comparisons (Appendix D–E), and Ghost Grad comparisons (Appendix A), were not extracted as separate rows. They concern SAE evaluation or training choices rather than individual-neuron polysemanticity.

untested.parts: No share of polysemantic MLP neurons measured.
Superposition as cause is assumed, not tested.
Activation-function comparisons concern SAE latents (ReLU, TopK, JumpReLU), not the base network's neurons.
The max-activation limitation concerns SAE feature scoring, not neuron polysemanticity judgments.

record.verdict_notes: The paper treats neuron polysemanticity as a premise ('Individual neurons in neural networks are polysemantic') citing Olah 2020 and Elhage 2022; no neuron-level data are reported. The reader's states for r3–r17 ('observed' and 'partial') should be cannot_determine, since no version applies.

versions.untested_parts: No vision model or individual vision neuron is tested.
No share of polysemantic MLP neurons in transformer language models is measured.
The study does not test whether capacity pressure causes neuron polysemanticity.
The study does not test neuron polysemanticity caused by initialization, regularization, or training noise.
The study compares SAE training choices and transformer components, not the share of polysemantic neurons or its effect on network performance.
The study evaluates SAE features on polysemous words, not whether canonical polysemantic neurons detect a shared feature or related jobs.
The study discusses a limitation of its own SAE evaluation metric but does not test how measurement choices change judgments of neuron polysemanticity.

rows.subject: GPT-2 small
rows.operation_detail: Compared cosine distance between representations for different-meaning polysemous contexts.

conditions.value: different meanings of the same target word

rows.value: Text reports that cosine distance was small, indicating less distinction between the contexts than for SAE features; numeric values are figure only.
rows.note: This measures base-model activations, not individual neurons; the figure's numeric values are not given in the text.
rows.check: Compares whole activation vectors (cosine distance), not individual neurons. Figure-only. The figure reference is confused: the text says Figure 3 (right) but the histogram is Figure 3 (left).

conditions.value: different meanings of the same target word

rows.baseline: LLM activations for the same contexts; numeric value not stated
rows.value: Text reports larger cosine distance than for LLM activations; numeric value is figure only.
rows.note: The authors interpret the larger distance as SAE features capturing differences between meanings. This is a result about SAE features, not neuron polysemanticity.
rows.check: SAE feature result. It does not bear on neuron polysemanticity.
